title: Proof
body_md:
A deficient three-by-two block remains deficient after adjoining any third column, contradicting the assumed three-minor condition. The two-by-three assertion follows by adjoining a row. The same facts hold for the adjoint, transpose and conjugate matrices.

Write \(a=|\operatorname{supp}x|\), \(d=|\operatorname{supp}y|\). If \(d=1\), nonzero entries of \(C\) give \(a=6\); if \(a=1\), apply the same argument to \(y=C^*x\). If \(d=2\) and \(a\le3\), the at least three zero coordinates of \(x\) give a rank-deficient three-by-two block. If \(a=2\) and \(d\le3\), use the adjoint argument. All other pairs have both sizes at least three. The only equality case remaining in that range is \((3,3)\), which is impossible: the three rows outside the support of \(x\) and the three columns supporting \(y\) form an invertible block annihilating \(y\). These observations prove both conclusions. \(\square
head: manual

label: eq:3.4
title: Proof
body_md:
At such a point, \(z_B=0\) and \(u_D=0\) give

\[
Mv_D=0,\qquad M^Tw_B=0. \tag{3.4}
\label{eq:3.4}\]

The flat block \(M\) has no zero entries; if singular, it has rank one. Both kernels in \hyperref[eq:3.4]{(3.4)} are one-dimensional, and each nonzero kernel vector has both coordinates nonzero. Choose these vectors, extend them by zero, and set \(z=Cv\), \(u=C^Tw\). An extra zero coordinate of \(z\) outside \(B\) would make a three-by-two block deficient. An extra zero coordinate of \(u\) outside \(D\) would make a two-by-three block deficient. Consequently the supports are exactly \(A=B^c\), \(E=D^c\), and every native and transformed product is zero. The choices of the two kernel vectors affect only the two projective scalings. Conversely the supports at a given point recover \(B,D\) and its block, proving injectivity. \(\square
head: manual

title: Proof
body_md:
Work first at pattern \((4,2,2,4)\) in projective affine charts. Represent a tangent vector by \(\delta z,\delta w\), set \(\delta v=C^*\delta z\), \(\delta u=C^T\delta w\), and put \(q=\delta t\). By \hyperref[eq:3.2]{(3.2)}, every index is allowed in the linearized equations. Since the supports are complementary, they give

\[
\delta w_i=q/z_i\ (i\in A),\qquad \delta z_i=q/w_i\ (i\in B),
\]

\[
\delta u_j=q/v_j\ (j\in D),\qquad \delta v_j=q/u_j\ (j\in E). \tag{3.6}
\label{eq:3.6}\]

The unchanged vector \(w\) supplies the decisive pairing:

\[
\sum_{i\in B}w_i\delta z_i
=w^T\delta z=(C^Tw)^T\delta v
=\sum_{j\in E}u_j\delta v_j.
\]

Using \hyperref[eq:3.6]{(3.6)}, the left side is \(2q\) and the right side is \(4q\). Hence \(q=0\). This uses the tangent equations of the full scheme; counting boundary points alone would not exclude a component leaving the boundary.

Now \(\delta w_A=\delta z_B=\delta u_D=\delta v_E=0\). The remaining equations reduce to

\[
M\delta v_D=0,\qquad M^T\delta w_B=0.
\]

Their kernels are the same one-dimensional spaces as in \hyperref[eq:3.4]{(3.4)}. Therefore \(\delta z\) is proportional to \(z\) and \(\delta w\) to \(w\). These are precisely the rescalings removed by the projective charts. The tangent vector is zero. At the second pattern the conjugate calculation under \hyperref[eq:3.5]{(3.5)}, or the direct pairing with \(4q=2q\), gives the same conclusion.

Let \(\mathfrak m\) be the maximal ideal of the Noetherian local ring at a boundary point. The zero tangent space means \(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2=0\). Nakayama's lemma gives \(\mathfrak m=0\), so the local ring is its residue field \(\mathbb C\). The point lies on no positive-dimensional component. Deleting the finitely many other irreducible components gives an open neighborhood supported at that point. Each such point is therefore reduced and isolated in the full scheme. \(\square
head: manual

title: Proof
body_md: If a point is fixed, choose representatives with \(w=\lambda\overline z\) for a nonzero scalar \(\lambda\). The product equations give \(\lambda|z_i|^2=t\) for all \(i\). Since \(z\ne0\), their common value cannot be zero; in particular \(z_0\ne0\). In the unique affine representatives, \(w=\overline z\), \(z_0=w_0=1\), and \(|z_i|=1\). The transformed products now read \(|v_j|^2=1\). Thus \(q=z/\sqrt6\) is a unit vector unbiased to \(I\) and \(C\). Conversely every such ray has a unique representative of this form with \(z_0=1\), and supplies this fixed point. Boundary patterns \hyperref[eq:3.3]{(3.3)} also directly show there are no fixed boundary points. \(\square
head: manual

title: Proof
body_md:
Every vertex has \(z^*z=6\). Six distinct pairwise orthogonal vertices therefore give six unit orthogonal columns \(z/\sqrt6\), hence a complete orthonormal basis of \(\mathbb C^6\). Conversely the columns of any actual companion basis supply six distinct vertices and every \(O\)-edge. Projective rays remove column phases; the unordered clique removes column permutations, and these are exactly the redundancies in this correspondence. For two cliques,

\[
\left|\left\langle z/\sqrt6,z'/\sqrt6\right\rangle\right|^2
=|z^*z'|^2/36,
\]

so mutual unbiasedness is precisely \(U\) for every cross pair. The same actual columns occur in all conditions. A shared vertex has squared unnormalized overlap \(36\) and fails \(U\); repeated vertices cannot belong to an \(O\)-clique. All conditions are invariant under unit column phases. This includes the case of no six-clique. No existence of a companion basis or quartet, and no assertion uniform over varying \(C\), is used. \(\square
head: manual

label: eq:4.4
title: Proof
body_md:
We compare the two ideals on the arrangement complement, then show that localization has not changed the ray algebra. Put \[
D_i=\frac{\partial\log\Phi_H}{\partial z_i}
=\sum_c\frac{\overline{h_{ic}}}{s_c}-z_i^{-1},
\qquad 1\le i<n.
\] Row orthogonality gives \[
\begin{split}
\sum_c\frac{\overline{h_{ic}}G_c}{s_c}
&=\sum_c\overline{h_{ic}}r_c
-n\sum_c\frac{\overline{h_{ic}}}{s_c}\\
&=nz_i^{-1}-n\sum_c\frac{\overline{h_{ic}}}{s_c}.
\end{split}
\] Hence \[
D_i=-\frac1n\sum_c\frac{\overline{h_{ic}}G_c}{s_c}.
\tag{4.4}
\label{eq:4.4}\] For the reverse inclusion define, for all \(0\le p<n\), \[
k_p=z_p\sum_c\frac{\overline{h_{pc}}}{s_c}-1.
\] Then \(k_i=z_iD_i\) for \(i>0\), and \[
\sum_pk_p=\sum_c\frac{s_c}{s_c}-n=0,\qquad
k_0=-\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}z_iD_i.
\] The preceding orthogonality calculation for every \(p\) gives \[
\sum_c\frac{\overline{h_{pc}}G_c}{s_c}=-n\,\frac{k_p}{z_p}.
\] Multiplying by \(h_{pc}\), summing in \(p\), and using column orthogonality yields \[
G_c=-s_c\sum_p h_{pc}\frac{k_p}{z_p}
=-s_c\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}(h_{ic}-z_i)D_i.
\tag{4.5}
\label{eq:4.5}\] Thus the two ideals agree in the localized ring. To return to the original Laurent quotient, observe that the localization removes no part of the ray algebra: modulo the \(G_c\), each \(s_c\) is already invertible, with inverse \(r_c/n\). This proves the full-algebra assertion.

On \(|z_i|=1\), one has \(r_c=\overline{s_c}\), so \(G_c=0\) means \(|s_c|^2=n\). Since \[
C^*(z/\sqrt n)=H^*z/n,
\] these are exactly the common-unbiased-vector equations. Parseval gives \[
\sum_c|s_c|^2=z^*HH^*z=n^2.
\] The arithmetic--geometric mean inequality now gives \[
\prod_c|s_c|^2\le
\left(\frac{\sum_c|s_c|^2}{n}\right)^n=n^n.
\] The denominator of \(\Phi_H\) has modulus one. Equality holds exactly when all \(|s_c|^2=n\), proving \hyperref[eq:4.3]{(4.3)}. \(\square
head: manual

label: eq:4.9
title: Proof
body_md:
All \(\gamma_i\) are nonzero and \(\gamma_0=1\), so \hyperref[eq:4.8]{(4.8)} is a Laurent automorphism preserving \(x_0=w_0=1\). For the common-ray input \(\overline C\), put \[
v=C^{\mathsf T}x,\qquad u=\overline C^{\mathsf T}w.
\] By \hyperref[eq:4.6]{(4.6)}, \[
v_k=\frac{U_{jk}}{\overline{B_{0j}}},\qquad
u_k=\frac{V_{jk}}{B_{0j}}.
\] Here the second identity uses \(w_i=B_{ij}z_i^{-1}/B_{0j}\), since \(B\) is flat. As \(|B_{0j}|^2=1/6\), \[
v_ku_k-1=6U_{jk}V_{jk}-1.
\tag{4.9}
\label{eq:4.9}\] This identifies the ideals themselves. The full fibre is obtained by quotienting this one-row algebra by the other row equations. Complex conjugation preserves nonvanishing of the middle minors, so \hyperref[result:theorem-3.1]{the boundary/finiteness theorem} applies to \(\overline C\). A quotient of a finite-dimensional algebra is finite-dimensional. \(\square
head: manual

label: eq:5.12
title: Proof
body_md:
The argument has two parts. The middle-minor hypotheses make the projective ray family finite, but a torus chart of that family need not remain finite over the coefficient ring. The ordered compatibility equations supply the missing control: the inverse identity of a complete collection would turn boundary escape into a forbidden dependence of boundary tensors. The full proof, including that independence argument, appears in \hyperref[appendix-dvr-complete-companions-cannot-escape]{Appendix B}. We give the mechanism here. The projective equations are \[
z_iw_i=t,\quad (Tz)_j(C^{\mathsf T}w)_j=t
\quad(i,j=1,\ldots,5),\qquad t=z_0w_0.
\tag{5.12}
\label{eq:5.12}\] The missing crossed zero equation follows from \(\sum_j(Tz)_j(C^{\mathsf T}w)_j=\sum_i z_iw_i=6t\). The ordinary middle-minor support argument and full tangent calculation work in every algebraically closed field of characteristic different from two and three. They give \hyperref[eq:5.11]{(5.11)}, reduced isolated boundary points, and finite projective fibres. The structure morphism of this projective \(R\)-scheme is proper and quasi-finite, hence finite.

The needed independence concerns the rank-one matrices \(z_rw_r^{\mathsf T}\), or outer products, of boundary vectors. It is proved in \hyperref[appendix-dvr6-independence-of-at-most-six-compatible-boundary-matrices]{Appendix B}, using both ordered bilinear compatibility equations, rather than inferred from isolatedness. Type-II row-ratio identities exclude a strip of rank-one \(2\times2\) blocks. The remaining mixed support configuration contradicts \[
\operatorname{tr}\bigl(C[A,E]T[E,A]\bigr)
=\sum_{a\in A,e\in E}C_{ae}T_{ea}=4/6=2/3.
\tag{5.13}
\label{eq:5.13}\] For a complete generic collection, choose primitive projective representatives, with integral coordinates and at least one unit coordinate in each vector, \(z_r,w_r\), and \(t_r=z_{0r}w_{0r}\). The ordered equations give the inverse identity of the complete square column matrix \[
\sum_{r=0}^5\frac{z_rw_r^{\mathsf T}}{t_r}=6I_6.
\tag{5.14}
\label{eq:5.14}\] If some \(t_r\) had positive valuation, multiply by a uniformizer to the largest of those valuations and reduce. The surviving tensors would give a nontrivial dependence among at most six compatible boundary points. The invertible boundary Jacobian prevents two generic members from colliding at one boundary point. Thus \hyperref[eq:5.13]{(5.13)} and the full independence argument rule out escape.

Excluding escape makes the torus locus of the finite projective compatible-tuple scheme closed as well as open. That locus is precisely the scheme of \(P_R\), with its entire scheme structure. Finite tensor products and quotients give \(Q_R\). Complete geometric special-fibre emptiness says its reduction modulo the uniformizer is zero; Nakayama gives the final zero-algebra implication. \hyperref[appendix-dvr-complete-companions-cannot-escape]{The appendix} supplies every support, block, collision, valuation and full-scheme step in this outline. \(\square
head: manual
name: mechanism

label: eq:6.3
title: Proof
body_md:
We first check that the symmetries preserve common unbiasedness, and then check orthogonality. The factorization \[
K_\eta=(I_m\otimes H_2)\operatorname{diag}_j(1,\bar\eta_j)(F_m\otimes I_2)
\] proves unitarity; the displayed entries prove flatness. If \(k_{\ell b}\) is its actual column, direct substitution gives \[
Dk_{\ell b}=k_{\ell+1,b},\qquad
Jk_{\ell0}=k_{-\ell,1},\qquad Jk_{\ell1}=-k_{-\ell,0}.
\tag{6.3}
\label{eq:6.3}\] The unitary \(D\) permutes the anchor rays, while \(J\) exchanges their two binary labels. Both also preserve the coordinate rays of \(I\). Since each \(\eta_j\) is unit and \(L\) is real with \(L^2=-I_2\), \(J\) is antiunitary and \[
J^2=-I,\qquad JD=D^{-1}J.
\tag{6.4}
\label{eq:6.4}\] For any anchor column \(k\), unitarity and antiunitarity give \[
|\langle k,Dg\rangle|=|\langle D^{-1}k,g\rangle|,\qquad
|\langle k,Jg\rangle|=|\langle J^{-1}k,g\rangle|.
\] Thus every iteration of \(D\) or \(J\) sends a common-unbiased vector to another one. Every column of \hyperref[eq:6.2]{(6.2)} is consequently unbiased to both anchors.

Orthogonality has two separate ingredients. Equal entry moduli in the fixed coordinate basis, or native flatness, give each block the same weight, \(\|g_j\|^2=\|Jg_j\|^2=1/m\); skew antiunitarity makes the two local directions orthogonal:

\[
g_j^*Jg_j=\bar\eta_j(\bar g_{j0}\bar g_{j1}-\bar g_{j1}\bar g_{j0})=0.
\] The equal block weights make the within-orbit sums Fourier characters, while the zero local pairing annihilates every mixed sum. For all \(r,s\in\mathbb Z/m\), \[
\langle D^rg,D^sg\rangle
=\langle D^rJg,D^sJg\rangle
=\frac1m\sum_j\omega^{j(s-r)}=\delta_{rs},\qquad
\langle D^rg,D^sJg\rangle=0.
\tag{6.5}
\label{eq:6.5}\] The complete Gram matrix is therefore the identity. The \(2m\) columns form a common-unbiased orthonormal basis whose first column is the prescribed \(g\). \(\square
head: manual

title: Proof
body_md:
\hyperref[result:theorem-6.1]{The completion theorem} needs one seed. \href{https://arxiv.org/abs/1408.5728v3}{Idel--Wolf, Theorem 2} supplies it: for every unitary \(U\), diagonal unitary matrices \(L_0,R_0\) make \(L_0UR_0\) have row and column sums one. Apply it to \(K_\eta^*\). Then \[
L_0K_\eta^*R_0\mathbf1=\mathbf1,\qquad
g=R_0\mathbf1/\sqrt{2m},\qquad
K_\eta^*g=L_0^*\mathbf1/\sqrt{2m}.
\] Both native and anchor coordinates are flat, so \hyperref[result:theorem-6.1]{Theorem 6.1} supplies a third basis. \(\square
head: manual

label: eq:7.4
title: Proof
body_md:
The native entries in \hyperref[eq:7.2]{(7.2)} already have the required modulus and unit norm. To test the other anchor, take its adjoint: \[
(K_\eta^*g)_{m0}=\frac13\sum_j\omega^{-jm}p_jc_j,\qquad
(K_\eta^*g)_{m1}=\frac i3\sum_j\omega^{-jm}\eta_jp_js_j.
\tag{7.4}
\label{eq:7.4}\] For any triple \(z\), define \(N(z)=\sum_j|z_j|^2\) and \(C(z)=\sum_jz_j\bar z_{j+1}\). Expansion yields \[
\left|\frac13\sum_j\omega^{-jm}z_j\right|^2
=\frac{N(z)+\omega^mC(z)+\omega^{-m}\overline{C(z)}}9.
\tag{7.5}
\label{eq:7.5}\] Comparison of the three Fourier coefficients shows that the squared moduli equal \(1/6\) precisely when \(N=3/2\) and both nonconstant coefficients vanish, that is, \(C=0\). Here \(pc=(p_jc_j)_j\) and \(\eta ps=(\eta_jp_js_j)_j\) denote entrywise products. Applying the formula to these two sequences, and using \(\sum s_j^2=3-\sum c_j^2\), gives the squared-norm equation and two correlation equations in \hyperref[eq:7.3]{(7.3)}.

Conversely, the raw coordinates represent every native-flat physical vector, with its own global phase. For such an \(h\), choose real \(u_j,v_j\) with \(\sqrt6h_{j0}=e^{iu_j},\sqrt6h_{j1}=e^{iv_j}\). Set \(\theta_j=(u_j-v_j)/2\), \(q_j=e^{i(u_j+v_j)/2}\), \(\sigma=q_0\), \(p_j=q_j/\sigma\). Then \(h=\sigma g\), \(p_0=1\), and \(\sigma\) is independent of every other seed's phase. Anchor flatness gives \hyperref[eq:7.3]{(7.3)}. The correlation equations also prevent vanishing sine or cosine amplitudes, which will justify the divisions in \hyperref[actual-clock-triples-and-their-conditional-companion-bridge]{Section 8}. If \(|z_j|\le1,N(z)=3/2,C(z)=0\), one zero is impossible. For example, \(z_0=0\) leaves \(z_1\bar z_2=0\), hence at most one nonzero entry and \(N(z)\le1\). Apply this to \(pc,\eta ps\). \(\square
head: manual

title: Proof
body_md:
The \(r\)-th column pair has native block \(\omega^{jr}W_j/\sqrt3\). Taking inner products gives the exponent \(j(s-r)\) and factor \(1/3\) in \hyperref[eq:7.9]{(7.9)}. Each difference \(s-r\) occurs for three ordered pairs, so each Fourier entry occurs three times.

The determinant-one form of each local frame product also couples the two columns of the Fourier sums. The products \(W_j(\alpha,p)^*W_j(\beta,q)\) have determinant one, hence form \(\begin{pmatrix}u_j&v_j\\-\bar v_j&\bar u_j\end{pmatrix}\). Consequently \[
(\mathcal F_m)_{11}=\overline{(\mathcal F_{-m})_{00}},\qquad
(\mathcal F_m)_{01}=-\overline{(\mathcal F_{-m})_{10}}.
\tag{7.10}
\label{eq:7.10}\] Flatness of the first column at all three Fourier labels therefore gives flatness of the second, with label reversal \(m\mapsto-m\). For a selected physical ray \(h=\sigma h_0\), \[
(E_\eta(g_0)^*h)_{(r,a)}=\sigma(\mathcal F_{-r})_{a,0}.
\tag{7.11}
\label{eq:7.11}\] Thus unbiasedness of one selected ray to \(E_\eta(g_0)\) supplies the first-column conditions, which imply all twelve conditions through \hyperref[eq:7.10]{(7.10)}. No original fourth basis is assumed in this calculation.

The two seeds retain independent global phases: if \(g=\rho g_0\), then \(E_\eta(g)=E_\eta(g_0)B_\rho\), where the diagonal of \(B_\rho\) is \(\rho\) on \(a=0\) and \(\bar\rho\) on \(a=1\). Thus actual overlaps are \(B_\rho^*[E_\eta(g_0)^*E_\eta(h_0)]B_\sigma\). Further unitary column monomials act by \(M^*[E_\eta(g_0)^*E_\eta(h_0)]N\), retaining their phases and labels. \(\square
head: manual

label: eq:7.13
title: Proof
body_md:
We begin with the restrictions on a single permitted profile. Put \[
v_j=\cos2\theta_j,\quad
P_j=\cos^2\theta_j=(1+v_j)/2,\quad
Q_j=\sin^2\theta_j=(1-v_j)/2,\quad
r=\sum_jv_j^2,\quad t=v_0v_1v_2.
\] Here \(P,Q\) are squared amplitudes; the seed phases are \(p_j\). The squared-norm equation gives \(\sum v_j=0\), \(\sum P_j=\sum Q_j=3/2\). Here \(e_1(P)=P_0+P_1+P_2\), \(e_2(P)=P_0P_1+P_1P_2+P_2P_0\), and \(e_3(P)=P_0P_1P_2\) are the elementary symmetric polynomials, with the same convention for \(Q\). The squared sides of the cosine-product triangle are \(P_0P_1,P_1P_2,P_2P_0\); its four Heron factors multiply to \[
2\sum_{\rm cyc}(P_0P_1)(P_1P_2)
-\sum_{\rm cyc}(P_0P_1)^2=4e_1(P)e_3(P)-e_2(P)^2.
\] Every weak triangle inequality makes the corresponding Heron factor nonnegative; equality and zero sides are allowed. Hence \(6e_3(P)-e_2(P)^2\ge0\), and likewise for \(Q\). Using \(\sum v_j=0\) gives \[
e_2(P)=e_2(Q)=\frac34-\frac r8,\quad
e_3(P)=\frac{1-r/2+t}{8},\quad
e_3(Q)=\frac{1-r/2-t}{8}.
\] Multiplication by 64 yields \(12-12r-r^2\pm48t\ge0\), so \[
r+4|t|+\frac{r^2}{12}\le1.
\tag{7.13}
\label{eq:7.13}\] In particular, \[
r+2|t|<1.
\tag{7.14}
\label{eq:7.14}\] For \(r>0\), the upper bound is \(1-2|t|-r^2/12<1\); for \(r=0\), \(t=0\). Also, \[
|v_j|<1/\sqrt2\quad\text{for each }j.
\tag{7.15}
\label{eq:7.15}\] Otherwise a sign reversal and index choice allow \(v_0=x\ge1/\sqrt2\). Write \(u=v_1v_2\); then \(v_1+v_2=-x\), \(r=2(x^2-u)\), \(|t|=x|u|\). If \(u\le0\), \(r+4|t|\ge2x^2\ge1\). If \(u\ge0\), \(r+4|t|=2x^2+(4x-2)u\ge1\), since \(x>1/2\). Both contradict \hyperref[eq:7.13]{(7.13)}, as \(r>0\) supplies the extra positive \(r^2/12\).

These strict estimates apply independently to each of the three profiles. Now form the real array whose row \(j\) is \[
X_j=\cos2\alpha_j,\quad Y_j=\cos2\beta_j,\quad
Z_j=\cos2(\beta_j-\alpha_j).
\] Each column satisfies \hyperref[eq:7.14]{(7.14)}--\hyperref[eq:7.15]{(7.15)}, while each row links the three angles at one native block. The cosine difference identity gives in each row \[
X_j^2+Y_j^2+Z_j^2-2X_jY_jZ_j=1.
\tag{7.16}
\label{eq:7.16}\] Indeed, square \(Z-XY=\sin2\alpha\,\sin2\beta\).

The row identity forces a negative product. To prove this, put \(a=|X_j|,b=|Y_j|,c=|Z_j|\), all below \(k=1/\sqrt2\). If the product were nonnegative, \hyperref[eq:7.16]{(7.16)} would give \(f(a,b,c)=1-a^2-b^2-c^2+2abc=0\). But \(f>0\) on \([0,k)^3\). Separate concavity lets us bound \(f\) from below by applying a chord bound in each coordinate. The resulting lower bound is the trilinear interpolation of its eight vertex values on \([0,k]^3\). Those values, by number of coordinates equal to \(k\), are \[
1,\qquad 1/2,\qquad0,\qquad(\sqrt2-1)/2.
\] The vertex values are nonnegative, and strict membership in the cube gives the positive origin value weight \((1-a/k)(1-b/k)(1-c/k)>0\). This contradicts \(f=0\), also excluding a zero row product. Thus every array entry is nonzero, and each row obeys \[
a^2+b^2+c^2+2abc=1,\qquad0<a,b,c<1/\sqrt2.
\tag{7.17}
\label{eq:7.17}\] Let \(A=\arccos a,B=\arccos b,C=\arccos c\), in \((0,\pi/2)\). The positive root of \hyperref[eq:7.17]{(7.17)} is \[
c=-ab+\sqrt{(1-a^2)(1-b^2)}.
\] Its positivity gives \(a^2+b^2<1\), hence \(\pi/2<A+B<\pi\). Therefore \(c=-\cos(A+B)=\cos(\pi-A-B)\), and \[
\arccos a+\arccos b+\arccos c=\pi.
\tag{7.18}
\label{eq:7.18}\] The same inverse cosines behave differently down a column. There, \hyperref[eq:7.14]{(7.14)} says \(a^2+b^2+c^2+2abc<1\). The increasing quadratic \(z^2+2abz+a^2+b^2-1\), \(z\ge0\), has the unique positive root \[
z_0=-ab+\sqrt{(1-a^2)(1-b^2)}
=\cos(\pi-\arccos a-\arccos b).
\] Here \(a^2+b^2<1\), and the strict column inequality gives \(c<z_0\). Thus \[
\arccos a+\arccos b+\arccos c>\pi.
\tag{7.19}
\label{eq:7.19}\] All entries used in the inverse cosines are positive by the row argument, so no endpoint has been excluded without justification. Summing the same nine arccosines by rows gives \(3\pi\), whereas summing them by columns gives more than \(3\pi\). This contradiction excludes the three profiles. The original signed angles have not been normalized; the arccosines are auxiliary comparison angles. \(\square
head: manual

label: eq:7.21
title: Proof
body_md:
The correlation equations for each seed already provide the amplitude conditions for \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\): each is a zero sum of three complex numbers, so its three magnitudes obey the weak triangle inequalities. It remains to extract the same conditions for their difference from the overlap equations. Put \(\delta=\beta-\alpha\), \(a_j=\bar p_jq_j\), \(b_j=\eta_jp_jq_j\). Direct multiplication gives \[
W_j(\alpha,p)^*W_j(\beta,q)
=\begin{pmatrix}
a_j\cos\delta_j&i\bar b_j\sin\delta_j\\
ib_j\sin\delta_j&\bar a_j\cos\delta_j
\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{7.21}
\label{eq:7.21}\] The overlap sums use the positive Fourier exponent in \hyperref[eq:7.8]{(7.8)}, giving \[
\left|\sum_j\omega^{jm}z_j\right|^2
=N(z)+\omega^{-m}C(z)+\omega^m\overline{C(z)}.
\] The three values are \(3/2\) exactly when \(N=3/2,C=0\). Apply this to the 00 and 10 entries in \hyperref[eq:7.21]{(7.21)}. Condition \hyperref[eq:7.20]{(7.20)}, with the \(1/3\) factor, yields \[
\sum_j\cos^2\delta_j=3/2,\quad
\sum_j\cos\delta_j\cos\delta_{j+1}a_j\bar a_{j+1}=0,\quad
\sum_j\sin\delta_j\sin\delta_{j+1}b_j\bar b_{j+1}=0.
\] The unit phases turn the two zero sums into weak triangle inequalities for \(\delta\). Thus all three profiles satisfy the forbidden conditions of \hyperref[result:theorem-7.3]{Theorem 7.3}. Only a necessary subset of the twelve overlap equations was needed for this contradiction; the hypothesis still comprises all twelve. By \hyperref[result:lemma-7.2]{Lemma 7.2}, the contradiction excludes two MU constructed completions, including independently phased columns. \(\square

label: eq:8.1
title: Proof
body_md:
Uniform joint probabilities determine the reduced density matrices strongly enough to constrain a pure \(h\). Its conditional qubit states will then contradict the three qubit bases. Suppose \(h\) exists and let \(\rho_2,\rho_3\) be its reduced density matrices. Summing the joint probabilities \(1/6\) over the other factor gives \[
\langle a_{jr},\rho_2a_{jr}\rangle=1/2,\qquad
\langle b_{jt},\rho_3b_{jt}\rangle=1/3
\quad(j=0,1,2).
\tag{8.1}
\label{eq:8.1}\] Put \(\sigma_j=|a_{j0}\rangle\langle a_{j0}|-|a_{j1}\rangle\langle a_{j1}|\). They are traceless Hermitian, square to \(I_2\), and have \(\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_j\sigma_\ell)=0\) for \(j\ne\ell\), by local unbiasedness. Here the Hilbert--Schmidt product of matrices \(A,B\) is \(\operatorname{Tr}(A^*B)\). Their squared norms are two, so they form an orthogonal real basis of the three-dimensional traceless Hermitian qubit space. The uniform qubit marginals in \hyperref[eq:8.1]{(8.1)} annihilate every traceless component of \(\rho_2\), forcing \[
\rho_2=I_2/2.
\tag{8.2}
\label{eq:8.2}\]

For each qutrit basis let \(\mathcal D_j\) be its two-dimensional real space of traceless Hermitian diagonal matrices. If \(P_{jt}=|b_{jt}\rangle\langle b_{jt}|\), then \[
\operatorname{Tr}[(P_{jt}-I_3/3)(P_{\ell s}-I_3/3)]
=|\langle b_{jt},b_{\ell s}\rangle|^2-1/3=0
\quad(j\ne\ell).
\] The four diagonal spaces are pairwise orthogonal and their dimensions sum to eight, exhausting the traceless Hermitian qutrit space. The first three uniform marginals in \hyperref[eq:8.1]{(8.1)} therefore leave \(\rho_3-I_3/3\) in \(\mathcal D_3\). Consequently \(\rho_3\) is diagonal in the \textbf{given} fourth basis \(B_3\), rather than merely in an unspecified eigenbasis.

We now use purity to recover the state from these marginal restrictions. Writing \(h=\sum M_{rt}e_r\otimes f_t\) gives \(\rho_2=MM^*\), \(\rho_3=(M^*M)^T\), with the same nonzero eigenvalues. The Schmidt rank is the rank of this coefficient matrix \(M\). By \hyperref[eq:8.2]{(8.2)}, \(\rho_3\) has spectrum \(\{1/2,1/2,0\}\). Exactly two original \(B_3\) columns \(v_a,v_b\) support it. Expansion in the given basis \(B_3\) yields orthonormal qubit vectors \(u,v\) with \[
h=(u\otimes v_a+v\otimes v_b)/\sqrt2.
\tag{8.3}
\label{eq:8.3}\] Because \(\rho_3\) is already diagonal in \(B_3\), the repeated eigenvalue \(1/2\) does not require replacing the given qutrit columns.

For each of the first three product bases, conditioning on a qutrit outcome now gives three qubit states with equilateral relative phases. Fix \(j=0,1,2\) and set \(A_t=\langle b_{jt},v_a\rangle\), \(B_t=\langle b_{jt},v_b\rangle\), \(\zeta_t=B_t/A_t\). All denominators have modulus \(1/\sqrt3\). The normalized conditional qubit vector is \[
\psi_t=(\sqrt3A_t)(u+\zeta_tv)/\sqrt2,\qquad|\zeta_t|=1.
\] Orthogonality gives \(\sum_t\bar A_tB_t=\frac13\sum_t\zeta_t=0\). Three unit numbers with zero sum are a rotated equilateral triple: \[
\{\zeta_0,\zeta_1,\zeta_2\}=\zeta_*\{1,\omega,\omega^2\}.
\tag{8.4}
\label{eq:8.4}\] To see this, divide by one entry. The others sum to \(-1\); their real parts are \(-1/2\), making them \(\omega,\omega^2\) in one order.

The conditional probability is \((1/6)/(1/3)=1/2\), so every \(\psi_t\) is unbiased to \(A_j\). Hence \(\langle\psi_t,\sigma_j\psi_t\rangle=0\). The two diagonal entries of \(\sigma_j\) in the orthonormal basis \(u,v\) sum to zero. With \(m_j=\langle u,\sigma_jv\rangle\), expansion gives \[
0=\operatorname{Re}(\zeta_tm_j).
\] Equation \hyperref[eq:8.4]{(8.4)} forces both \(\operatorname{Re}(\zeta_*m_j)=0\) and \(\operatorname{Re}(\omega\zeta_*m_j)=0\). If \(\zeta_*m_j=iy\), \(y\in\mathbb R\), the latter is \(-\sqrt3y/2=0\); hence \(m_j=0\). For each \(j\), the three phase directions force the off-diagonal entry \(m_j\) to vanish. Thus all three \(\sigma_j\) are diagonal in the same qubit basis \(u,v\). Each is a real multiple of \(|u\rangle\langle u|-|v\rangle\langle v|\), and squaring to identity makes the multiple \(\pm1\). Two then have Hilbert--Schmidt product \(\pm2\), contradicting their orthogonality. The conclusion concerns pure rays; no mixed-state obstruction is claimed. \(\square

title: Proof
body_md: We first locate the two original clock orbits and describe their complement. The rank of the correlation-coefficient matrix then determines the companion, apart from the product alternative. Normalize \(\eta_0=1\) by \hyperref[eq:7.1]{(7.1)}, retaining all phases. Each native-flat vector has three distinct \(D\)-rays: if \(D^rg\) were proportional to \(g\), its three nonzero blocks would force \(\omega^{rj}\) to be constant, hence \(r=0\). Thus the six invariant rays of \(V\) are exactly two selected three-orbits. Choose any original seed \(g\) from one. Its orbit is orthonormal by \hyperref[result:theorem-6.1]{Theorem 6.1}.

label: eq:9.5
title: Proof
body_md:
We first identify the localized companion, then apply one common change of coordinates. Each \(U_j\) is unitary by its displayed norm condition. The two columns at each frequency in \hyperref[eq:9.4]{(9.4)} are orthonormal, so \(C_\nu\) is unitary; its native entries have modulus \(1/\sqrt6\). Put \[
B_j=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\\nu_j&-\nu_j\end{pmatrix},
\quad B=\operatorname{diag}_jB_j,\quad
P e_{(i,a)}=e_{(-i,a)}.
\] Then \hyperref[eq:9.4]{(9.4)} is precisely \(C_\nu=TBP\). The factorization identifies the common unitary \(A=B^*T^*=P C_\nu^*\) that sends the original companion to coordinate rays. Apply it to all three bases and any proposed ray. Direct multiplication gives \[
AC_\nu=P,\qquad AI=B^*T^*,\qquad
AS=B^*\operatorname{diag}_j(U_j)T^*.
\tag{9.5}
\label{eq:9.5}\] Right multiplication of the first anchor by \(P\) restores \(I\). Since \(B_j^*=H_2\operatorname{diag}(1,\bar\nu_j)\) and \(Q^*=QP_{\rm rev}\), where \(P_{\rm rev}e_n=e_{-n}\) and \(P=P_{\rm rev}\otimes I_2\), \[
B^*T^*=K_\nu P.
\] The right column permutation restores the second anchor to \(K_\nu\), with label \(m=-n\); it changes the order of its original rays. For \(e=\nu_0\ne1\), normalize \(\eta_j=\nu_j/e\) by the second-binary-column phases in \hyperref[eq:7.1]{(7.1)}. When \(\nu_0=1\), this normalization is the identity and \(\eta=\nu\).

The transported third basis is \[
V=B^*\operatorname{diag}_j(U_j)(Q^*\otimes I_2),\qquad
V_{j;(n,a)}=\omega^{-jn}B_j^*U_je_a/\sqrt3.
\] Multiplication by \(D\) changes \(\omega^{-jn}\) to \(\omega^{-j(n-1)}\), sending the original column \((n,a)\) exactly to \((n-1,a)\). Thus the transported third basis has \(D\)-invariant original rays. All three MU conditions and any common-ray condition survive the same \(A\), so \hyperref[result:theorem-8.2]{Theorem 8.2} applies to the transported original triple \(I,K_\eta,V\). The inverse common operation is \(A^*=TB\), with the displayed right permutations and phases reversed. Hence an extra ray for the original triple would give one for the transported triple, a contradiction. Every transition is between the given bases. \(\square
